Shipley.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Aire Valley
s1loc: Shipley carries a heritage visitor economy anchored by Saltaire, the Victorian model village built by Sir Titus Salt from 1851 and inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. Salts Mill, the vast Italianate textile works designed by Lockwood and Mawson, now holds the largest public collection of David Hockney's work in its 1853 galleries, with shops, restaurants and the planned streets around Victoria Road drawing visitors across the year.

The leisure and activity layer runs through Roberts Park, opened in 1871 across the River Aire for the mill workers, with its cricket pitch, bandstand and Half Moon Cafe. Shipley Glen, a sloped Victorian pleasure ground of rock and heather, is reached by the Shipley Glen Tramway of 1895, the oldest working cable tramway in the country, while Hirst Wood nature reserve and Northcliffe Woods give walkers green space close to the centre.

Heritage and culture trace the canal age through the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, which threads past Saltaire and Hirst Lock with its towpath walks and the ornate Bird Cage kissing gate at the lost Milner Field estate. The Saltaire United Reformed Church, the costumed guided tours of the village and the annual Saltaire Festival each September fill the calendar with concerts, art trails and events across the conservation streets.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house base serving heritage and business trade, with a guide scene built around the World Heritage village. Shipley and Saltaire stations on the Airedale Line link the town to Leeds, Bradford and Skipton, and the canal towpath runs on to Bingley and Keighley, so operators here handle steady weekend and seasonal crowds drawn to Salts Mill, the moors and the wider Aire Valley.

Frome.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of east Somerset
s1loc: Frome draws a steady visitor economy on the strength of its medieval townscape, with over 300 listed buildings strung across the old wool and cloth town. Cheap Street, with its leat running down the middle of the cobbles, the steep cobbled climb of Catherine Hill, and the 14th-century St John the Baptist Church anchor the historic core, while Stony Street and the surrounding lanes pull visitors in for a townscape unlike anywhere else in the county.

The leisure and activity layer spreads out from the town centre, with Rodden Meadow giving a riverside wildflower walk beside the River Frome and Victoria Park offering play areas and green space close in. Just to the south, Longleat Safari and Adventure Park, the Elizabethan house and drive-through safari at the Longleat estate, draws coach and family trade across the warmer months, keeping operators busy through the season.

Heritage and culture run through the independent-shop quarter and a packed events calendar. Black Swan Arts, the town's contemporary gallery and craft centre in a former coaching inn, and the Cheese and Grain live-music and events venue host year-round programmes, while the monthly Frome Independent market, the July Frome Festival and the September Frome Agricultural and Cheese Show fill the streets with food, craft and music stalls.

Underpinning it all is a guest-house, inn and hotel base serving heritage and festival visitors, with a guide scene built around the listed town and the surrounding estates. Frome station on the Heart of Wessex Line links the town toward Bath, Bristol and Westbury, and the road network carries day-trippers out to Longleat, Stourhead and the Mendip Hills, so operators here handle seasonal market crowds and country-house trade alike.

Gosforth.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north Newcastle
s1loc: Gosforth, a suburb two miles north of Newcastle city centre, carries a visitor draw led by Newcastle Racecourse on the 812-acre High Gosforth Park estate. The Grade 1 National Hunt and all-weather track, the only one in the country with a straight mile, hosts more than sixty fixtures a year, headlined by the Northumberland Plate, which transferred here from the Town Moor in 1881, with conference and banqueting facilities and the Border Minstrel public house on the estate.

The leisure and activity layer runs through Gosforth Central Park, with its bowling greens, tennis courts and playground, and the Gosforth Nature Reserve set within Gosforth Park, where 61 hectares of woodland, wetland and reedbed managed by the Natural History Society of Northumbria record over 1,600 species, from roe deer and otters to bitterns and kingfishers. Parklands Golf complex and woodland walks at High Gosforth Park add to the outdoor offer.

Heritage and culture reach into the wider city from the suburb. The Town Moor, a thousand acres of common land stretching from Gosforth toward the city centre, hosts the Hoppings each June, one of Europe's largest travelling funfairs, dating in its modern form to 1882. Gosforth's St Nicholas parish church and its stained-glass collection, the High Street's cafes and the nearby Jesmond Dene river park give visitors a rich local round.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house base serving business, racing and stopover trade, with a guide scene built around the racecourse and the city. The Tyne and Wear Metro, run from its depot in Gosforth since the system opened in 1980, links the suburb to Newcastle Central, the coast and Newcastle International Airport in around 25 minutes, so operators here handle event crowds, business visitors and seasonal city trade across the year.

Pontypool.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Torfaen
s1loc: Pontypool anchors the Torfaen visitor economy at the head of the eastern South Wales valleys, led by Pontypool Park, the 64-hectare People's Park laid out around the former Hanbury family estate. The Folly Tower, first built by John Hanbury in 1762, demolished in the Second World War and rebuilt as a replica in 1994, and the nearby Shell Grotto commissioned by Capel Hanbury Leigh in the 1830s open at weekends from May to September above the valley.

The leisure and activity layer runs through the park's children's play area, tennis courts, pitch and putt, bowls and dry ski slope, with the rugby pitch home to Pontypool RFC. A short drive out, Llandegfedd Lake and Watersports Centre between Pontypool and Usk offers windsurfing, sailing, kayaking, paddleboarding and trout fishing across 434 acres of reservoir and woodland designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest, drawing activity trade from March to October.

Heritage and culture run through the town's industrial past. The Torfaen Museum, housed in the former stables of the Hanbury estate within Pontypool Park, and the restored Italian Gardens tell the area's story, while just to the north Blaenavon holds the Big Pit National Coal Museum and the wider Blaenavon Industrial Landscape, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with Goytre Wharf canal visitor centre adding a 200-year-old industrial heritage stop nearby.

Underpinning it all is a guest-house and inn base across the valley, with a guide and day-trip scene reaching out to the canals, the reservoir and the mining heritage of the hills. Pontypool and New Inn station on the Welsh Marches Line links the town toward Newport and Cardiff, and the A4042 carries visitors up the valley toward Abergavenny and the Brecon Beacons, so operators here handle seasonal outdoor trade and heritage crowds alike.

Bilston.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Black Country
s1loc: Bilston, a market town in the City of Wolverhampton two and a half miles south-east of the city centre, carries a Black Country visitor draw rooted in its enamelling and ironworking past. First recorded as Bilsatena in AD 985, the town is led by Bilston Craft Gallery, which displays works of local significance from the eighteenth century alongside a temporary exhibition space, and St Leonard's Church, the 1825 rebuilding by Francis Godwin in the manner of John Soane.

The leisure and activity layer runs through the town's parks and green spaces alongside the Birmingham Canal, opened in parts between 1769 and 1772 to carry coal from Bilston to Birmingham, whose towpaths now serve walkers and cyclists. The Bilston branch of the Walsall Canal and the wider Black Country canal network give the area waterside routes, while local recreation grounds keep families and activity operators working across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Grade II listed Bilston Town Hall and the market, with Church Street the early market place where the commissioners built the market hall in 1892. The Robin 2 on Mount Pleasant, a 700-capacity live music venue that has hosted names from the Red Hot Chili Peppers to local heroes Slade, anchors the entertainment offer, with its Noddy's Bar named for the Slade frontman drawing gig crowds year-round.

Underpinning it all is a guest-house and inn base serving the wider city, with a guide and day-trip scene built around the Black Country canals and heritage. The West Midlands Metro tram line runs through Bilston Central toward Wolverhampton and Birmingham, and the road network links the town to Willenhall, Walsall and the Black Country Living Museum, so operators here handle event crowds, market trade and visitors heading for the region's attractions across the year.

Sedgley.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Black Country ridge
s1loc: Sedgley sits on a ridge in the Black Country, its marquee draw the Sedgley Beacon, which rises to 778 feet above sea level as one of the highest points in the region. The Beacon Hill tower gives views across the Black Country, Cannock Chase and Birmingham to the east and toward the Wrekin, the Clee Hills and the Malvern Hills to the west, with the hills of north Staffordshire and Derbyshire visible on the clearest days.

The leisure and activity layer runs across the ridge's green spaces and out to the wider borough. Just to the south at Dudley, the Wren's Nest National Nature Reserve, a geological Site of Special Scientific Interest and Scheduled Ancient Monument, has yielded over 700 types of fossil, 86 of them found nowhere else on Earth, while the Dudley Canal and Tunnel Trust runs underground boat trips through the limestone caverns nearby.

Heritage and culture centre on All Saints' Church, rebuilt in 1829 in Neo-Gothic style and paid for by the Earl of Dudley, seating well over a thousand and carrying an organ from Westminster Abbey, and on the Bull Ring, the central junction named for the bull-baiting held there until the sport was outlawed in 1835. Sedgley Hall Farm, the old courthouse and the conservation streets give the town a distinct historic character.

Underpinning it all is an inn and guest-house base serving the wider conurbation, with a guide and day-trip scene built around the Beacon, the geology and the canals. The road network links Sedgley to Dudley, Wolverhampton and Bilston, with the Black Country Living Museum and the West Midlands Metro a short trip out, so operators here handle steady visitor flow drawn to the ridge views, the nature reserves and the heritage of the surrounding towns.

Tipton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Black Country canals
s1loc: Tipton carries a Black Country visitor draw built on water, once known as the Venice of the Midlands. The Birmingham Canal arrived in 1770, and over the following fifty years the town grew the centre of a dense network with over thirteen miles of navigable waterway within its boundaries. The towpaths of the surviving Old and New Birmingham Canal Navigations Main Lines now serve walkers, cyclists and anglers across the year, with a residential canal basin recreated at the nearby museum.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Sheepwash Urban Park, a Local Nature Reserve of about 37 hectares laid out south of Great Bridge on former landfill and brickworks land, with its pools, John's Lane and Sheepwash Lane entrances drawing walkers and birdwatchers. The wider canal towpaths, recreation grounds and green corridors give families and activity operators outdoor space close to the centre through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture trace the town's industrial story. The parish church of St Martin in Lower Church Lane, a plain Georgian brick structure built under an Act of Parliament in 1797, anchors the historic core, while the canal festival tradition around Owen Street and the wider Black Country Living Museum at nearby Dudley, recreating early-twentieth-century life in original buildings many transported from Tipton itself, give visitors a strong sense of the industrial past.

Underpinning it all is an inn and guest-house base serving the conurbation, with a guide and day-trip scene built around the canals and the museum. Tipton and Dudley Port stations on the line through the Black Country, and the bus links from Owen Street out to the Black Country Living Museum, bring visitors in, with the West Midlands Metro extension running close by toward Dudley and Wednesbury, so operators here handle steady towpath, festival and heritage trade across the year.
